prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a family owned business called GCP, which produces golf clubs in the United States. They used to produce clubs that were easy to use, so most of their customers are beginner players. They recently received a patent for a new club that would enhance the performance of amateurs and professionals alike. Product innovation is paramount in this industry and they want help capitalizing on this development with a strong product launch.
prompt.question: Help GCP plan a strong product launch for its new patented golf club. The case will walk through: (1) analyzing the market, (2) deciding whether to build a new plant or expand the current one, (3) identifying other issues in the decision, (4) identifying possible problems with the expansion, and (5) pricing an insurance policy to protect against construction risk.

clarifying_info.q: What production methods does GCP currently use?
clarifying_info.a: GCP currently uses liquid production only. Some competitors use solid production as well.

clarifying_info.q: What is the estimated demand for the new club?
clarifying_info.a: Demand is estimated at 60,000 sets over the next few years.

clarifying_info.q: What are the details of building a new plant vs. expanding?
clarifying_info.a: Both options require a $2M initial one-time investment. New plant: Machine line I = 2,000 sets/month at $12.5M; Machine line II = 1,250 sets/month at $8M; maximum 3 lines. Existing plant expansion: Machine line I = 1,250 sets/month at $8M; Machine line II = 7,500 sets/year at $5.5M. All machines are equally durable.

exhibits.title: Golf Club Sets Sold by Segment (2007-2011)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of golf club sets sold per year from 2007 to 2011 (2009-2011 are estimates), broken into four segments: Solid (for professionals), Solid (for amateurs), Other Liquid, and Top 10 Liquid.

data.approximate_total_range: ~2,000 to ~6,500+ sets across the years shown

framework: Assess market attractiveness: size, growth rate, segmentation, competitive dynamics
Evaluate production options: compare costs and capacity for new plant vs. expansion
Identify qualitative/strategic factors beyond cost that affect the plant decision
Anticipate key execution risks of the chosen expansion path
Quantify financial exposure and insurance cost to protect against construction risk

questions.prompt: Phase 1: What do you observe about the market from the chart? Does being one of the top liquid producers matter?
questions.guidance: 1) The market has been growing rapidly — more than 100% in two years — making it clearly attractive. 2) The top 10 liquid producers command a huge market share, so scale matters. Reasons: easier to invest in product innovation; economies of scale in production, distribution, and advertising.

questions.prompt: Phase 2: Should GCP build a new, additional plant or expand the current plant to meet estimated demand of 60,000 sets?
questions.guidance: Ignore the equal $2M one-time investment (same in both cases). Compare machine costs and capacity needed to produce 60,000 sets. New plant optimum: 2 type-I + 1 type-II machines. Expanding optimum: 4 type-I machines. Costs are roughly the same (~$32-33M), so qualitative factors must drive the final recommendation.

math.setup: Demand = 60,000 sets. One-time investment = $2M (same for both, ignore in comparison). New plant: Type I = 2,000 sets/month @ $12.5M; Type II = 1,250 sets/month @ $8M; max 3 lines. Expansion: Type I = 1,250 sets/month @ $8M; Type II = 7,500 sets/year = 625 sets/month @ $5.5M.
steps: New plant option A (2×Type I + 1×Type II): capacity = 2*2,000*12 + 1,250*12 = 48,000 + 15,000 = 63,000 sets; cost = 2*12.5 + 8 = $33M
New plant option B (3×Type I): capacity = 3*2,000*12 = 72,000 sets; cost = 3*12.5 = $37.5M — more expensive, eliminate
Expansion: note Type I at expansion = 1,250/month = 15,000/year; Type II = 7,500/year — Type I is far more cost-effective
Expansion with 4×Type I: capacity = 4*1,250*12 = 60,000 sets (exactly meets demand); cost = 4*8 = $32M
math.answer: New plant (optimal mix): $33M for 63,000 sets capacity. Expansion (4×Type I): $32M for exactly 60,000 sets. Costs are roughly the same; ~$1M difference could be offset by future capacity needs of the new plant.

questions.prompt: Phase 3: Given that calculated costs are roughly equal, what other issues would you analyze? What are the pros and cons of each option?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorm. Strong answers cover multiple dimensions: Management/Admin (one plant = lower labor and G&A costs); Product quality (one plant = easier to maintain consistent standards); Distribution (two locations may reduce shipping costs); Event/catastrophic risk (two plants = diversified insurance and lower per-plant risk); Future capacity (new plant has ~3,000 sets/year more headroom); Time to implement; Impact on current production lines during construction.

questions.prompt: Phase 4: The CEO decided to expand the current plant. Assuming market estimates are 100% accurate, what are the two main issues that keep him up at night?
questions.guidance: Timing: Product innovation is paramount and the market is fast-growing, so a late launch could forfeit first-mover advantage. Costs: Construction costs could escalate after the decision is made, eroding projected margins. Follow-up: The CEO can protect himself by purchasing an insurance policy against each of these risks.

questions.prompt: Phase 5: What would the insurance price be given the following assumptions? GCP has contracts to sell 60,000 sets at $500 each. If GCP cannot produce more than 90% of 60,000 sets in the next eight months, they lose 10% of the contracts (probability 20%). If GCP produces 90%+ in eight months, they lose nothing. The insurer operates with a 10% margin.
questions.guidance: Calculate expected loss from insurer's perspective, then gross up for margin. Expected loss = probability of shortfall * value of lost contracts. Price = expected expense / (1 - margin).

math.setup: Revenue at risk = 10% of 60,000 sets * $500/set = $3,000,000. Probability of shortfall = 20%. Insurer margin = 10%, so expected expense = 90% of premium.

brainstorming.prompt: Given that the calculated costs for a new plant vs. expansion are roughly the same, what other issues would you want to analyze? What are the pros and cons of each option?

categories.name: Management / Admin
ideas: Single plant means lower labor overhead and G&A
Two plants require duplicate management layers and coordination

categories.name: Product Quality
ideas: One plant makes it easier to maintain a single quality standard
Two plants risk quality divergence between facilities

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Two geographically separate plants may lower shipping costs to different regions
Single plant may face higher logistics costs to distant markets

categories.name: Event / Catastrophic Risk
ideas: Two plants diversify the risk of a fire, flood, or other site-specific disaster
Insurance premiums would be lower per plant when risk is spread across two sites

categories.name: Future Capacity
ideas: New plant has ~3,000 more sets/year capacity headroom for future demand growth
Expansion exactly meets current demand forecast with no buffer

categories.name: Implementation
ideas: Time to build a new plant vs. expand may differ; speed to market matters given fast market growth
Expansion may disrupt current production lines for existing club models

recommendation: Expand the current plant using 4 Type-I machines at a cost of $32M, which exactly meets the 60,000-set demand forecast
Costs are nearly identical to a new plant ($32M vs. $33M), but expansion avoids duplicate management overhead and quality-control complexity
risks: Construction cost overruns could erode the economic case — mitigate with insurance ($666,667 premium)
Timing risk: if expansion is delayed, GCP may miss critical early-mover window in a fast-growing market
If demand significantly exceeds 60,000 sets, the expansion provides no buffer; the new plant option would have offered ~3,000 extra sets/year headroom
next_steps: Negotiate a fixed-price construction contract to cap cost escalation
Purchase insurance policy (calculated at ~$667K) to hedge production shortfall risk
Develop a detailed project timeline with milestones to ensure on-time launch
Monitor market growth vs. forecast; establish a trigger to revisit new-plant option if demand exceeds capacity
